content: Many medications, including chloroquine, can affect the heart's rhythm, potentially causing a condition known as QT prolongation. This condition can lead to serious irregular heartbeats. The risk of QT prolongation increases if you have certain medical conditions, such as low levels of potassium or magnesium in the blood, or if you are taking other medications that also prolong the QT interval. Diuretics (water pills) or conditions like severe sweating, diarrhea, or vomiting can further increase this risk. Certain vaccines, such as the rabies or cholera vaccines, may not work as effectively if administered while you are taking chloroquine. It is important to inform your healthcare provider about all medications you are taking before receiving any vaccines. If someone overdoses on chloroquine and experiences severe symptoms like loss of consciousness or difficulty breathing, call emergency services (911 in the U.S.) immediately. For non-emergency overdoses, contact a poison control center. U.S. residents can call 1-800-222-1222, and Canadian residents can call 1-844-764-7669. If you are taking chloroquine for an extended period, regular medical and laboratory tests are necessary. These may include eye exams, reflex tests, liver and kidney function tests, EKGs, and complete blood counts. Ensure you attend all scheduled medical and lab appointments. When traveling to areas at risk for malaria, use protective measures such as wearing protective clothing, applying insect repellent, and sleeping under bed nets. Stay indoors or in screened areas whenever possible. If you are using chloroquine to prevent or treat malaria, use it only for your current travel or condition as prescribed. If you miss a dose of chloroquine, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is close to the time of your next dose, skip the missed dose and resume your regular dosing schedule. Do not double the dose to catch up. Store chloroquine at room temperature, away from light and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Do not flush medications down the toilet or pour them into a drain unless instructed to do so. Properly discard this product when it is expired or no longer needed. This medication may cause side effects such as nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps, headache, and diarrhea. It may also cause low blood sugar (hypoglycemia), which can present as symptoms like sudden sweating, shaking, hunger, blurred vision, dizziness, or tingling in the hands or feet. If you have diabetes, monitor your blood sugar levels regularly and report any abnormalities to your doctor. Chloroquine can cause serious eye or vision problems, especially with long-term use or high doses. Inform your doctor immediately if you experience any changes in vision. This medication may also increase sensitivity to sunlight, so limit sun exposure, avoid tanning booths and sunlamps, and use sunscreen and protective clothing when outdoors. During pregnancy, chloroquine should only be used when clearly needed, as it passes into breast milk. Discuss the risks and benefits with your doctor if you are pregnant or breastfeeding. Drug interactions may alter how your medications work or increase the risk of serious side effects. Keep a list of all the products you use, including prescription and non-prescription drugs and herbal products, and share it with your doctor and pharmacist. Always consult your healthcare professional for complete information about this medication and your specific health needs.
